standard.title: Media influence on health
standard.description: investigate how media and influential people impact attitudes, beliefs, decisions and behaviours in relation to health, safety, relationships and wellbeing
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have investigated different sources and types of health information and how these apply to health choices (Y5-6). They can identify and apply health information but have not yet been expected to investigate the mechanisms by which media and influential figures shape attitudes and beliefs — not just inform decisions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate how media and influential people impact attitudes, beliefs, decisions and behaviours in relation to health, safety, relationships and wellbeing.

nodes.label: Understanding how media shapes health attitudes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how different types of media sources and influential people can shape attitudes and beliefs about health, safety, relationships and wellbeing — beyond just providing information.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one media source and explain one way it shapes attitudes or beliefs about health (not just provides information about it).
nodes.typical_width: Explain how different source types (news, bloggers, influencers, social media advertising) operate differently as attitude and belief shapers; distinguish between informing, persuading and normalising as media mechanisms; connect media exposure to attitude formation across multiple health domains.
wider: Analyse how social media algorithms shape what health information young people see, and evaluate what media literacy strategies help students navigate this curated environment
Explore how messages related to food are portrayed in media and how this shapes decision-making about health and wellbeing, examining both explicit messaging and normalisation through representation
nodes.hinge_reason: The descriptor asks students to investigate impact on attitudes, beliefs, decisions and behaviours — not just to evaluate source credibility. Students who only understand media as information provision cannot investigate attitudinal and behavioural influence, which is the primary focus of this descriptor.

response_modes.reason: Distinguish between media as information source and media as attitude/belief shaper. Explicitly model the mechanism: exposure → normalisation → attitude → behaviour. Without this distinction, students evaluate credibility but do not investigate influence.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one media source and explains how it operates as a shaper of attitudes or beliefs
Distinguishes between providing information and shaping attitudes in at least one example

nodes.label: Analysing credibility and investigating influence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the credibility, validity and relevance of health messages from media and influential people, and explain how these messages may influence health-related attitudes, beliefs and decisions.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse the credibility of one health message from a media source and explain one way it might influence attitudes or decisions.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse credibility, validity and relevance across a range of source types; investigate how sexual relationship messages, body image messages and health information are constructed across different media forms; apply credible information to health-related decisions.
wider: Explore health campaigns targeting First Nations Australian young people (Deadly Choices, Don't Make Smokes Your Story, Yarn Safe) and analyse the messages, strategies and cultural framing used to promote health
Analyse how messages related to sexual relationships are portrayed in different media forms and evaluate how they may influence the way people act within relationships

response_modes.reason: Credibility analysis and influence investigation across multiple health domains (food, sexual health, body image, mental health) prevents students from developing a single-domain framework that does not generalise.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations health campaign analysis provides genuine insight into how culturally grounded health messaging works differently from mainstream media — a meaningful analytical extension that broadens students' understanding of health communication.
success_criteria: Analyses at least one health message from a media source using credibility, validity or relevance as a criterion
Explains how the message might influence attitudes, beliefs or decisions

nodes.label: Applying critical media literacy to health decisions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply critical analysis of media health messages to inform their own health-related decisions and evaluate the impact of media influence on themselves and others.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply an analysis of a media health message to inform at least one health-related decision or evaluate one way media has influenced their own or others' health attitudes.
nodes.typical_width: Apply credibility analysis and influence understanding to health decisions across multiple domains; evaluate the impact of media influence on health attitudes and behaviours; explore how to access reliable health information sources for specific health questions.
wider: Evaluate the accessibility and reliability of health information sources that target young people in relation to their health, wellbeing, body, sexuality and relationships — building a personal framework for evaluating sources
Investigate how algorithmic curation of health content creates echo chambers and evaluate strategies for diversifying the health information young people encounter

response_modes.reason: Applied media literacy integrates source analysis, influence mechanism understanding and personal decision-making — the application should explicitly connect the analytical skills built in prior nodes to concrete health decision contexts.

success_criteria: Applies analysis of a media health message to inform or evaluate a health-related decision
Evaluates at least one way media influence has affected health attitudes, beliefs or behaviours in a specific context
